title: What is operating leverage, and why do fixed costs make profit swing?
description: How fixed and variable costs shape profit, what operating leverage means, and how to use it in profitability and investment cases.
hook: Operating leverage is how strongly profit reacts to a change in sales, and it comes from fixed costs: a business with mostly fixed costs keeps almost every extra dollar of sales as profit, but loses almost every lost dollar too. That is why two companies with the same revenue and profit today can react completely differently when sales move, and why a small fall in volume can explain a big fall in profit in a case.
body:
Fixed and variable, quickly

Fixed costs stay the same whatever the volume, within a range and over a given period: rent, salaried staff, equipment, insurance. Variable costs rise with each unit sold: ingredients, packaging, delivery, sales commissions, card fees. Contribution is price minus variable cost per unit: what each sale adds towards covering fixed costs and then profit.

A worked example: same profit, very different risk

Two illustrative companies both have $1M of revenue and $100k of profit.

Company ACompany B
Fixed costs$800k$100k
Variable costs$100k$800k
Profit today$100k$100k
Profit if sales rise 10%$190k (+90%)$120k (+20%)
Profit if sales fall 10%$10k (−90%)$80k (−20%)

When sales rise 10%, A's variable costs rise only $10k, so profit almost doubles. B's rise $80k, so profit grows just 20%. When sales fall 10%, A's profit is nearly wiped out. Same revenue, same profit, very different risk.

Two quick ways to measure it

  • Degree of operating leverage = contribution ÷ profit. A: $900k ÷ $100k = 9, so a 1% change in sales moves profit about 9%. B: $200k ÷ $100k = 2.
  • Break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin. A: $800k ÷ 90% ≈ $889k, so sales can fall only about 11% before A loses money. B: $100k ÷ 20% = $500k, so B has a 50% cushion. (See the break-even shortcut.)

Airlines, hotels, cinemas, telecoms and software companies are classic high-leverage businesses. Distributors and staffing agencies, where most cost is goods or people bought per order, sit nearer to B.

Why it matters in a case

  • Profitability cases: in a high fixed-cost business, a small drop in volume can explain a big drop in profit. Check volume before hunting for rising costs (see the profitability framework).
  • Capacity and investment cases: filling empty capacity (seats, rooms, machine time) is very profitable, so ask about utilisation before building more.
  • Pricing: in high fixed-cost businesses, discounts to fill spare capacity can make sense, as long as price stays above variable cost and does not pull down full-price sales.
  • Outsourcing and make-or-buy: outsourcing turns fixed costs into variable ones. That lowers risk at low volume and costs more at high volume.

Fixed depends on the time horizon

Over a week, rent and salaried staff are fixed. Over five years, the business can close a site or restructure, so almost everything becomes variable. Some costs are step-fixed: a restaurant needs one more chef once covers pass a certain level. Before labelling a cost, ask what decision you are making and over what period. "Fixed over the next year, but we could exit the lease in three" is the kind of precision interviewers notice.

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Profit fell 60%, so costs must have gone up a lot. Let's look at each cost line."
Strong: "Since most of the cinema's costs are fixed, a 10% fall in attendance would cut profit far more than 10%. Before looking at cost lines, I'd like to check whether volumes fell."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming profit moves in proportion to sales. It only does if every cost is variable.
  • Labelling costs without a time frame. Fixed and variable depend on the period and the range of volume.
  • Accepting a discount below variable cost "to fill capacity". Every such sale loses money.
  • Forgetting the upside. High operating leverage is a risk in a downturn, and a strength when volumes grow.

Practise

1. A cinema has $6M of fixed costs and sells 900,000 tickets a year at $10, with $2 of variable cost per ticket. What happens to profit if attendance falls 10%?

Show the answer

Profit today: 900,000 × $8 − $6M = $1.2M. After the fall: 810,000 × $8 − $6M = $480k, down 60%. Degree of operating leverage: $7.2M ÷ $1.2M = 6, so a 10% volume fall becomes a 60% profit fall.

2. A half-empty hotel is offered a group booking at $70 a night. Its normal rate is $150 and the variable cost per occupied room is $30. Should it accept?

Show the answer

Each room adds $70 − $30 = $40 of contribution, so yes, provided the rooms would otherwise stay empty and the deal does not tempt full-price guests to ask for the same rate.

3. Making a part in-house costs $2M a year of fixed cost plus $5 per unit. A supplier charges $15 per unit. At what volume are they equal, and which is cheaper at 150,000 and 300,000 units?

Show the answer

Equal when $2M + $5 × units = $15 × units, so at $2M ÷ $10 = 200,000 units. At 150,000: in-house $2.75M versus $2.25M outsourced, so outsource. At 300,000: in-house $3.5M versus $4.5M, so make it. The more uncertain the volume, the more the supplier's flexibility is worth.
